questions.prompt: A 7B model in 16 bits decodes one sequence on a card with 400 GB/s of bandwidth reached at 80%. About how long is one decode step, ignoring the cache?
options: About 4 ms
About 44 ms
About 88 ms
About 22 ms
questions.explanation: 14 GB of weights read at 320 GB/s takes about 44 ms; at batch 1 the step waits on memory.
misconceptions: Divides by the operation rate as if decode were bound by arithmetic
Counts four bytes per weight, as in 32-bit training
Counts one byte per weight, as if the model were in 8 bits

questions.prompt: A visitor pastes a 6,000-token event terms document. Which resource mostly sets the time to its first token on Musamir's L4?
options: The accelerator's arithmetic rate
The network between the visitor and the node
Memory bandwidth, because the weights are read for every token
The size of the cache
questions.explanation: A prefill processes all 6,000 tokens in one pass that shares one read of the weights, so it is bound by arithmetic.
misconceptions: Blames transport for compute time: the tokens are small
Assumes the prompt is read token by token as in decode
Confuses whether it fits with how fast it runs

questions.prompt: A model has 40 layers, 40 query heads and 8 key-value heads of size 128, with a 16-bit cache. How many bytes of cache does one token take?
options: 819,200 bytes
81,920 bytes
40,960 bytes
163,840 bytes
questions.explanation: 2 × 40 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 163,840 bytes; only the key-value heads are stored.
misconceptions: Sizes with the 40 query heads as if every head were stored
Stores only keys, or only values
Counts one byte per value and keys only

questions.prompt: Your prediction says 18 conversations of 2,000 tokens fit; the engine holds 12 and preempts. The model and length are right. What did the prediction most likely leave out?
options: The speed of the accelerator
The query heads
The engine's reserve for activations and the memory-utilisation limit
The tokenizer's vocabulary
questions.explanation: The cache gets only what is left after the utilisation limit, the weights and the reserve; leaving those out overstates the cache.
misconceptions: Speed does not change how many conversations fit
Would make the prediction four times too low, not too high
The vocabulary affects weights, already counted

questions.prompt: Musamir in 16 bits holds about 12 conversations of 2,000 tokens, and decoding reaches the ridge point only at about 246 sequences. What binds the baseline's concurrency?
options: The sequence cap of the engine
Cache memory: the batch never grows enough to use the arithmetic
The network bandwidth
Arithmetic: the card is too slow
questions.explanation: The cache fills at about 12 sequences, far below the 246 at which decode would use the arithmetic: memory capacity binds.
misconceptions: Blames a setting that could be raised without more room
Moves the problem outside the node
Reads a memory-bound step as a slow processor

questions.prompt: In 100 seconds an engine finishes 60 requests; 45 met the whole objective (TTFT, TPOT and stall), 10 missed only the TPOT limit, 5 missed only the TTFT limit. What is the goodput?
options: 0.45 requests per second
0.60 requests per second
0.55 requests per second
0.50 requests per second
questions.explanation: Only requests meeting the whole objective count: 45 in 100 s is 0.45 per second.
misconceptions: Counts throughput, every finished request
Counts the requests that met TTFT
Counts the requests that met TPOT

questions.prompt: Two configurations have the same mean TTFT of 1.4 s. A has a p90 of 1.9 s, B a p90 of 4.2 s. Against Musamir's objective, which serves visitors better?
options: Neither can be judged without throughput
They are equal: the means are the same
B, because its spread shows it handles bursts
A: more of its requests meet the 2.0 s objective
questions.explanation: The objective is per request; A's 90th percentile is under 2.0 s, B's is not.
misconceptions: Throughput does not tell who was served well
Treats the mean as the objective
Reads a long tail as a strength

questions.prompt: A curve shows throughput rising from 0.25 to 0.44 requests per second between 4 and 16 users, while goodput falls from 0.23 to 0.00. Where should the engine be run?
options: Anywhere: the objective is met on average
At 16 users, where throughput is highest
Near 4 users, with admission control holding it there
At 1 user, where every request meets the objective
questions.explanation: The knee of goodput is the operating point; beyond it extra load is served late.
misconceptions: Averages away a per-request objective
Optimises the busy measure, not the served one
Wastes the batching that is free until the knee

questions.prompt: One run of a new setting gives a p90 TTFT 0.3 s lower than the baseline, whose three runs spread by 0.6 s. What do you report?
options: An improvement of 0.3 s
No difference established yet; repeat the new setting three times
A regression, because the result is noisy
An improvement, because throughput held
questions.explanation: A difference smaller than the run-to-run spread is not evidence until repeated.
misconceptions: Takes one run as a measurement
Treats noise as evidence of harm
Swaps the question for another measure

questions.prompt: Why can a closed-loop test at 16 users look survivable when the real evening peak is not?
options: Closed-loop users wait for each answer, so the load eases when the engine slows
Closed-loop tests use shorter prompts
Open-loop tests add network delay
Closed-loop tests skip the warm-up
questions.explanation: Real arrivals keep coming whatever the engine does; a closed loop throttles itself.
misconceptions: The prompts are the same in both
Neither adds delay by itself
Warm-up is dropped in both

questions.prompt: At 8 visitors an engine shows 4 sequences running (its cap is 4), 4 waiting, and 22% of the cache in use. The TTFT p90 is 9 s. What is the diagnosis?
options: Preemption under cache pressure: lower the cap
Prefill interference: switch on chunked prefill
The card is too slow: add a second card
Queueing at the sequence cap: raise the cap
questions.explanation: The engine runs at its cap with a queue while most of the cache is free: the cap refuses work the card has room for.
misconceptions: Preemption needs a nearly full cache; here it is four-fifths empty
Interference shows as stalls in running answers, not as a queue
Buys hardware for a limit set by one setting

questions.prompt: A deployment with a cap of 48 shows the cache 96% in use and the preemption counter rising by about 10 per 100 requests. Which change should come first?
options: Switch off prefix caching
Raise the cap to 64 so waiting requests are admitted
Lower the cap or give the cache more memory
Raise the token budget per step
questions.explanation: Answers outgrow the blocks the engine admitted them with; fewer sequences or more blocks stop the evictions and the recomputation.
misconceptions: Shared blocks save memory; removing them adds pressure
More admissions mean more evictions when the cache is the limit
The budget limits work per step, not the blocks answers hold

questions.prompt: Chat answers freeze for about two seconds whenever a long document arrives, yet the chat TPOT p90 is 110 ms. Why does TPOT miss the problem?
options: TPOT is measured on the server, the freeze on the client
A two-second gap spread over 150 tokens moves the mean pace by only about 13 ms
TPOT ignores the first token, where the freeze happens
The freeze is in the network, which TPOT does not include
questions.explanation: TPOT is a mean over the answer; one long gap barely moves it, which is why the objective also limits the longest stall.
misconceptions: Both can be measured from the client's stream
The freezes happen mid-answer, after the first token
The gap comes from one long engine step, not transport

questions.prompt: With chunked prefill, budgets of 512, 1,024 and 2,048 tokens give chat stall p90 of 0.18, 0.35 and 0.68 s and document TTFT p90 of 2.47, 2.20 and 2.09 s. Under Musamir's objective, which budget do you choose?
options: 1,024: both clocks meet the objective with margin on the stall
2,048, because documents start fastest
8,192, to finish documents in one step
512, because chat stalls are smallest
questions.explanation: 512 pushes document TTFT over 2.0 s; 2,048 meets both but with less margin under the 1 s stall; 1,024 balances the two.
misconceptions: Defensible on these numbers but trades away the stall margin for 0.1 s
Brings back the stalls chunking was switched on to remove
Optimises one clock and breaks the other

questions.prompt: In a closed-loop test with 6 users, caps of 6, 8 and 12 give identical results. What explains it?
options: The cache limits the engine to six sequences
The token budget caps the batch at six
The simulator ignores the cap above 6
Six users never put more than six requests in the engine at once
questions.explanation: Each closed-loop user waits for an answer before sending again, so the engine never holds more requests than users.
misconceptions: The cache holds far more than six sequences at this load
The budget limits tokens per step, not sequences
The cap works; there is simply nothing more to admit

questions.prompt: A prompt is built as: request id, system instructions, tenant rules, conversation history, question. Prefix caching hits almost nothing. What change fixes it?
options: Switch to a block size of 32 tokens
Raise the cache's memory
Move the request id after the history, next to the question
Shorten the system instructions
questions.explanation: A block is reused only if every token before it is identical; a changing first token makes every block a miss.
misconceptions: Larger blocks make reuse harder, not easier
The blocks miss because their hashes differ, not because they were evicted
A shorter shared part is still never reused behind a changing id

questions.prompt: Why does a per-tenant cache salt barely lower the hit rate in Lab 2.3?
options: The salt is ignored by the engine for short prompts
Most reuse is within a tenant: its own rules, documents and conversation history
The salt is applied only to the last block
Salting doubles the cache size
questions.explanation: Only the shared base text was reused across tenants; tenants mostly reuse their own blocks, which the salt keeps.
misconceptions: The salt changes every block's hash, whatever the length
It is mixed into the first block, so it changes every hash after it
The salt changes hashes, not memory

questions.prompt: The base instructions are public text. Rawya still forbids reusing cache blocks across tenants. Which reason holds?
options: Reuse is visible in timing, and the rule must not depend on judging which text is sensitive
Cross-tenant reuse slows the engine down
Prefix caching is not allowed with Arabic text
Reused blocks give wrong answers to the other tenant
questions.explanation: A faster first token reveals that another tenant's prompt started the same way; a salt per tenant closes that channel at little cost.
misconceptions: Reuse makes requests faster, not slower
Reuse works on tokens in any language
Prefix reuse never changes an answer; the model still writes it

questions.prompt: A semantic cache at threshold 0.90 hits 3.8% of questions, and every hit in the sample was a wrong answer. Hanadi's limit is one wrong answer in 1,000. What do you recommend?
options: Lower the threshold to get more right hits
Use it for Arabic only
Raise the threshold to 0.95
No semantic cache on text alone; keep the prefix cache
questions.explanation: The wrong pairs differ in one slot and are the most similar; no threshold removes them before the useful hits.
misconceptions: Adds hits, and wrong answers with them
Arabic was the worse language at 0.90
Leaves the near-identical wrong pairs, the last to fall

questions.prompt: A question reads: "Can I move booking LW-482913 to Friday? Call me on 0551234567." What should a semantic cache do with it?
options: Skip masking, since the lookup is internal
Store it with the numbers masked
Mask it for the lookup and never store its answer
Store it as written, since it is the visitor's own data
questions.explanation: Masking keeps numbers out of the index and logs; an answer written for one booking must never be served to another visitor.
misconceptions: The index and logs are where personal data leak
The answer itself was written for that booking and would be served to others
A cached answer is served to other visitors

questions.prompt: An 8B-parameter model moves from 16-bit to 8-bit weights on a 24 GB card. Roughly where does the freed memory go, and what does it buy?
options: Nowhere: the engine keeps the reservation
About 8 GB more cache, so several times more conversations fit
Faster arithmetic only; memory is unchanged
A larger reserve for activations
questions.explanation: The weights shrink by about 8 GB; the engine gives what is left after weights and reserve to the cache, which more than triples here.
misconceptions: The engine sizes the cache from what remains at start
FP8 also speeds arithmetic on cards that support it, but the memory saving is real
The reserve is fixed; the cache takes the rest

questions.prompt: A 4-bit variant scores 0.833 in English (floor 0.81) and 0.693 in Arabic (floor 0.73), and has the best goodput. What is the decision?
options: Reject it: it fails the Arabic floor; serve a variant that passes both
Ship it to English visitors only and keep 16 bits for Arabic, at no extra cost
Ship it: goodput matters more at the peak
Ship it: its average over both languages is 0.76
questions.explanation: The floors are per language; a variant that misses one does not pass, however fast it is.
misconceptions: Two models mean two pools of cards: a cost, not free
Capacity does not buy back quality under the floor
An average hides the language that fails

questions.prompt: Two cache formats were scored on the same 103 long Arabic items. Their separate 95% intervals overlap. What should you compute before concluding there is no loss?
options: Separate intervals at 99% instead
The English score on the same items
The mean of the two scores
A paired difference over the same items, with its interval
questions.explanation: Pairing removes the variation the two variants share; its interval can lie below zero when separate intervals overlap.
misconceptions: Wider separate intervals overlap more, not less
Another language does not test this one
A mean of two scores says nothing about their difference

questions.prompt: A draft model is accepted with probability 0.5 per token and proposes 3 tokens. About how many tokens does the base model emit per verification step?
questions.explanation: (1 - 0.5^4) / (1 - 0.5) = 0.9375 / 0.5 = 1.875 tokens per step, before counting the draft's own time.
misconceptions: Adds the base model's token to a draft that is always accepted
Counts only the accepted share of drafted tokens, without the base model's own token
Assumes every drafted token is accepted

questions.prompt: Routing easy requests to a distilled model holds both floors at threshold 0.4 (Arabic 0.737, floor 0.73) and at 0.5 (Arabic 0.733). The set has 300 items per language. Which threshold do you serve?
options: 0.5: it holds both floors and costs less
0.4: it holds both floors with a margin the set can still detect
0.6: the cost falls further
No routing: any loss is unacceptable
questions.explanation: 0.3 points over the floor is far inside the noise of 300 items; 0.4 keeps more margin at a small extra cost.
misconceptions: Defensible on the rule alone but leaves no margin for drift on new traffic
At 0.6 Arabic falls under its floor
The floors already define the acceptable loss

questions.prompt: With chunked prefill, two cards together keep the longest pause at 0.18 s and serve 96.5% of requests; split into a prefill and a decode card, 0.13 s and 93.9%. The objective allows a 1.0 s pause. What do you deploy?
options: Both phases on both cards: the shorter pause buys nothing under this objective
The split, with a second prefill card bought for it
One card only, since both layouts pass
The split: its pauses are shorter
questions.explanation: Disaggregation pays when a decode limit is tighter than a chunked step; here the objective allows 1.0 s and together serves more.
misconceptions: Adds cost to fix a problem the objective does not have
Two cards were needed for the load; passing on two says nothing about one
Optimises a clock that already meets its limit

questions.prompt: A prompt of 5,000 tokens has a cache of 73,728 bytes per token. The link between prefill and decode moves 20 GB/s. About how long does the transfer take?
options: About 180 ms
About 1.8 s
About 2 ms
About 18 ms
questions.explanation: 5,000 × 73,728 = 369 MB; at 20 GB/s that is about 18 ms.
misconceptions: Uses 2 GB/s, a factor of ten too slow
Mixes megabytes and gigabytes
Drops a factor of ten in the bytes

questions.prompt: A router hashes the tenant to pick one of three replicas. One replica shows 30 requests waiting and a full cache; the other two are almost idle. What is wrong?
options: The sequence cap is too high on the busy replica
The replicas are too small
Placement: the largest tenant always lands on one replica
The cache salt prevents sharing between replicas
questions.explanation: Two idle replicas and one drowning one is a hot spot: route by conversation with a load limit instead.
misconceptions: The cap does not create the imbalance
Total capacity is ample; it is unevenly used
Replicas never share cache blocks, salted or not

questions.prompt: A replica needs 8 minutes to start and the evening demand rises steeply. Which scaling signal keeps the worst hour above the objective at the lowest cost?
options: Requests waiting in the queue
The request rate, with headroom, and at least one replica
A fixed number of replicas for the peak, all day
The request rate with a minimum of zero replicas
questions.explanation: The rate rises before the queue does, and the headroom covers the minutes a new replica needs to start.
misconceptions: Reacts only once visitors wait, then overshoots during the cold start
Meets the objective at more than twice the cost
Leaves the first morning visitors waiting a whole cold start for almost no saving

questions.prompt: Over a day the node costs 107 SAR and 40,000 requests met the objective; a hosted API would charge 0.00105 SAR per request. What is the node's cost per successful request, and which is cheaper?
options: 0.00268 SAR; the hosted API
0.00268 SAR; the node
0.000268 SAR; the node
0.0268 SAR; the hosted API
questions.explanation: 107 / 40,000 = 0.00268 SAR per successful request, about 2.5 times the hosted price.
misconceptions: Computes correctly and compares the wrong way
Divides by ten times the requests
Divides by a tenth of the requests
